t.2.12.1: Seeing the descendant of Ikṣvāku tormented by grief for his son, fallen senseless upon the ground and writhing, that wicked woman spoke these words to him.
t.2.12.2: What is this? Having made me a promise, why do you lie dejected on the ground as if you had committed a sin? You ought to stand by your word.
t.2.12.3: People who know dharma say that truth is the highest dharma; and it is in reliance on truth that you have been urged by me toward dharma.
t.2.12.4: O king, Śaibya, lord of the earth, having promised his own body to the hawk, gave it to the bird and attained the highest state.
t.2.12.5: Thus indeed did the glorious Alarka, when a brāhmaṇa who had mastered the Vedas begged of him, pluck out his own two eyes and give them away without a troubled mind.
t.2.12.6: The lord of rivers, holding to truth, keeps even to the slightest limit; out of regard for truth, at the appointed time he does not overstep his own shore.
t.2.12.7: And if you do not honor this pact of mine, noble one, then, forsaken, I will give up my life before your very eyes.
t.2.12.8: Thus urged by Kaikeyī, who pressed him without hesitation, the king could not free himself from the noose, just as Bali could not loosen the noose made by Indra.
t.2.12.10: The king, his eyes clouded with distress as though he could not see, steadied himself with difficulty through sheer fortitude and spoke these words to Kaikeyī.
t.2.12.9: His heart reeling and his face drained of color, he became like a draught ox struggling caught between the yoke and the wheel.
t.2.12.11: O wicked woman, that hand of yours, consecrated with mantras, which I clasped before the sacred fire, I now renounce, and together with you I renounce your son as well, though he is my own offspring.
t.2.12.12: Then Kaikeyī, wicked in her conduct, skilled with words and overcome with rage, once more spoke harsh words to the king.
t.2.12.14: Having established my son in the kingdom, having made Rāma a forest-dweller, and having rid me of my rival, you will have accomplished your duty.
t.2.12.13: Why do you speak these words, O king, that are like the torment of poison? You ought to have your son Rāma brought here, unharmed.
t.2.12.15: Like a fine horse goaded by a sharp whip, the king, urged on again and again, spoke these words to Kaikeyī.
t.2.12.16: I am bound by the bond of dharma, and my mind is lost. I wish to see Rāma, my beloved eldest son, who is devoted to dharma.
t.2.12.17: Having heard these words of the king, Kaikeyī immediately thereafter herself said to the charioteer, "Go, bring Rāma here."
t.2.12.18: Then the glorious and righteous king, his joy over his son now sunk and his eyes red with grief, looked up at the charioteer and spoke.
t.2.12.20: When the lord of the earth, out of his dejection, could not himself speak, then Kaikeyī, skilled in counsel, replied to Sumantra.
t.2.12.19: Having heard the king's piteous lament and seen him so wretched, Sumantra, his palms joined in reverence, withdrew a little from that place together with those beside him.
t.2.12.21: "Sumantra, I will see Rāma; quickly bring the handsome one here." And he, thinking this to be auspicious, rejoiced in his heart.
t.2.12.22: Urged on by her to make haste, Sumantra thought: "Clearly Rāma, who knows dharma, will come here for the sake of his consecration."
t.2.12.23: Having thus made up his mind, the charioteer of great splendour went forth again with great joy, eager to see Rāghava.
t.2.12.24: Then, having swiftly come out in front, and looking upon the kings gathered at the gate, he saw the citizens of various kinds and of great wealth who had arrived and, approaching the gate, stood waiting there.
